messages.content: Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6.

function.name: statistics_calculate_p_value
function.description: Calculate the p-value for a t-test on a single sample from a population. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

sample_mean.description: The mean of the sample data. This is a float type value.

population_mean.description: The mean of the population data. This is a float type value.

sample_std_dev.description: The standard deviation of the sample data. This is a float type value.

sample_size.description: The size of the sample data.

two_tailed.description: Whether the test is two-tailed. If not provided, default is true.

message.content:
**Standard error (the “standard deviation” of the sampling distribution of the mean)**  

\[
SE = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}
\]

where  
- \(s = 1.4\) (sample standard deviation)  
- \(n = 40\) (sample size)

\[
SE = \frac{1.4}{\sqrt{40}} = \frac{1.4}{6.3249} \approx 0.221
\]

So the standard deviation of the null‑hypothesis test (i.e., the standard error of the mean under the null) is **≈ 0.22**.
message.reasoning:
The user asks: "Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6."

They want the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test. That likely refers to the standard error of the mean under the null hypothesis? Usually, the standard error of the sample mean is s / sqrt(n). But they mention "standard deviation of the null hypothesis test" maybe they want the standard error of the sampling distribution of the mean under null. That would be population standard deviation? But we only have sample standard deviation. For a t-test, we use sample standard deviation. So standard error = sample_std_dev / sqrt(sample_size) = 1.4 / sqrt(40). sqrt(40) ≈ 6.3249. 1.4 / 6.3249 ≈ 0.2213. So standard error ~0.221.

But maybe they want the standard deviation of the null distribution of the test statistic? For a t-test, the test statistic t = (sample_mean - population_mean) / (s / sqrt(n)). The denominator is the standard error. So the standard deviation of the null distribution of t is sqrt(n-1)/(sqrt(n-1))? Actually t distribution has variance n-1/(n-3) for df>2. But maybe they want the standard error.

Given the phrasing: "standard deviation of the null hypothesis test" might refer to the standard error of the mean under null. So answer: 0.221.

We can also compute the t-statistic: (98.2-98.6)/0.221 = -0.4/0.221 = -1.809. But they didn't ask for t.

Thus answer: approximately 0.221. Provide explanation.
